subject: microbiology
title: Cell Lines, Embryonated Egg, Haemagglutination, Interference and Antigenic Change

steps.tx: **Cell culture systems** include primary cells directly from tissue, diploid finite lines that senesce after passages, and continuous lines derived from tumours or immortalisation. Different viruses require different cells and incubation temperatures. Rhinovirus grows better at cooler upper airway temperatures, whereas many respiratory viruses use epithelial lines at core temperature. Cell choice is therefore a diagnostic variable, not a laboratory afterthought.
steps.say: The right cell line and temperature decide whether a virus grows at all.

left.title: Culture types
points: Primary monkey kidney historically broad susceptibility
Human diploid fibroblasts support CMV
Continuous lines simplify maintenance
Shell vial centrifugation speeds detection

right.title: Detection layers
points: Cytopathic effect observation
Immunofluorescent staining before CPE
Haemadsorption for haemagglutinating viruses
NAAT often replaces culture for speed

steps.tx: The **embryonated egg** offers several inoculation routes: chorioallantoic membrane for pox lesions, allantoic cavity for influenza and mumps growth, amniotic cavity for primary influenza isolation, and yolk sac historically for rickettsiae and chlamydiae. Influenza vaccine production still uses eggs widely, though egg adaptation can alter haemagglutinin antigenicity. Cell based and recombinant vaccines reduce that mismatch risk.
steps.say: Egg compartments were living culture flasks, and influenza still uses the allantoic cavity at scale.

left.title: Routes
points: Chorioallantoic membrane: pocks from poxviruses and HSV
Allantoic cavity: influenza and mumps replication
Amniotic cavity: sensitive primary influenza isolation
Yolk sac: historic intracellular bacteria culture

right.title: Modern relevance
points: Egg grown influenza vaccines are common
Egg allergy no longer blocks influenza vaccination in most guidance
Egg adaptation may reduce vaccine match
Cell and recombinant platforms avoid egg mutations

steps.tx: **Haemagglutination** occurs when viral surface proteins crosslink red blood cells. Influenza haemagglutinin binds sialic acid on erythrocytes, producing a lattice in a well. Antibody that blocks this is measured by haemagglutination inhibition, which historically guides influenza serology and vaccine strain work. Some viruses elute by neuraminidase destroying receptors, reversing agglutination over time.
steps.say: Haemagglutination is a visible receptor binding assay, and inhibition measures functional antibody.

left.title: Direct haemagglutination
points: Viral particles bridge red cells
Used to titrate influenza in culture fluid
Species of red cell can affect result
A diffuse mat rather than a button is positive

right.title: Inhibition test
points: Specific antibody blocks viral attachment
Used for influenza and rubella immunity historically
Requires standardised antigen dose
Paired titres show seroconversion

steps.tx: **Viral interference** is the phenomenon in which infection by one virus reduces replication of another in the same cell or host, often through interferon and resource competition. Rubella interference in monkey kidney cells was once exploited to detect rubella by challenging with a cytopathic enterovirus. Interference also shapes live vaccine scheduling and sequential viral infections, although simultaneous coinfections remain common.
steps.say: One virus can defend a cell against another by triggering interferon and occupying resources.

left.title: Mechanisms
points: Interferon induced antiviral state
Receptor blockade or downregulation
Competition for cellular machinery
Defective interfering particles compete for replication

right.title: Applications
points: Historic rubella detection by enterovirus challenge
Spacing some live viral vaccines
Interpreting sequential respiratory detections
Interferon defects cause severe viral susceptibility

steps.tx: **Antigenic drift** is gradual point mutation in influenza surface glycoproteins, especially haemagglutinin, allowing partial escape from population immunity and yearly vaccine updates. **Antigenic shift** is abrupt reassortment of segmented influenza genomes in a coinfected cell, exchanging whole segments and potentially generating pandemic strains with novel haemagglutinin or neuraminidase. Shift requires segmentation; drift occurs in many RNA viruses at different rates.
steps.say: Drift edits a few letters; shift swaps entire genome chapters in influenza.

left.title: Drift
points: Point mutations accumulate
Seasonal epidemics continue
Vaccine strains updated regularly
Antibody escape is partial

right.title: Shift
points: Reassortment of eight influenza segments
Human and avian viruses can coinfect swine or humans
Novel subtype can seed a pandemic
Only segmented viruses can reassort this way

steps.tx: Laboratory animal inoculation once isolated viruses and tested neurovirulence, but ethics, cost and molecular tools displaced most uses. Modern virus detection relies on **NAAT, antigen tests and sequencing**, while culture remains important for phenotypic resistance, novel virus characterisation and vaccine manufacture. Biosafety level follows transmission route and severity, not simply whether a specimen contains virus.
steps.say: PCR names most viruses today; culture still answers what the isolate actually does.
